strengths: Novel application of affordance-aware textual descriptions to 3D hand reconstruction, extending beyond categorical labels to capture rich object properties, interactions, and intentions
Well-motivated two-step description generation pipeline using chain-of-thought reasoning (VLM parsing followed by LLM summarization) that improves upon naive direct captioning
Consistent experimental improvements across all occlusion levels, with substantial 25% error reduction under heavy occlusion (4.9mm), addressing a practically important scenario
Principled approach to occlusion detection combining ray-casting for self-occlusion and SAM2 masking for object-occlusion, with targeted refinement of only uncertain joints
Clear presentation with effective visualizations; good demonstration of controllability showing the model responds to affordance variations (Figure 5)
Practical focus on severe occlusion scenarios relevant to VR/AR and robotic manipulation applications
weaknesses: Critical dependency on ground truth grasp taxonomy from HOGraspNet rather than predicting it with the VLM, directly undermining the claim of using VLMs for rich contextual knowledge. Grasp taxonomy classification is acknowledged as 'highly challenging' but no solution is proposed, creating a significant gap between the stated contribution and actual implementation

Limited evaluation scope: single-dataset evaluation (HOGraspNet only) without cross-dataset validation; only 1/10 of dataset used (~150k images); evaluation on only 300 instances in Table 1. Raises concerns about generalization beyond this specific benchmark

Modest average improvement of only 0.23mm across all occlusion levels (8.51→8.28mm), with negligible gains at low occlusion (7.69→7.67mm). Significant improvements concentrate in high-occlusion regime, limiting general applicability

Missing critical ablation studies: (1) two-step description vs. direct generation, (2) individual affordance element contributions (which matters most?), (3) refinement strategy components, (4) sensitivity to description quality. These ablations are essential to validate design choices

Insufficient baseline comparisons: only HaMeR and a weakened InterHandGen variant without text conditioning. No comparison with other context-aware, semantic, or affordance-based hand pose estimation methods. The unexplained degradation of unconditional InterHandGen at low occlusion deserves investigation

Incomplete training details and reproducibility concerns: sparse descriptions of diffusion model training (dataset composition, loss functions, hyperparameters), no discussion of computational costs, no mention of code availability, no quantification of VLM/LLM inference overhead at test time

VLM robustness not analyzed: no evaluation of sensitivity to VLM description errors, no comparison of different VLMs or prompts, no analysis of error propagation from VLM through the pipeline. Heavy reliance on off-the-shelf QwenVL2.5 and Mistral-7B without validation

Limited technical novelty: diffusion architecture adapted from InterHandGen [12], refinement strategy from prior work [16], uses off-the-shelf VLM/LLM/CLIP components. Primary novelty is in application combination rather than methodological innovation

Generalization concerns: SAM2-based object-occlusion detection may not transfer across datasets; no evaluation with different hand pose initializers, object categories, or camera views beyond HOGraspNet; all experiments use HaMeR as sole baseline estimator

No failure case analysis or discussion of when affordance guidance might conflict with visual evidence; no investigation of failure modes or failure rate; qualitative analysis limited to cherry-picked examples and narrow affordance variations (object size only)

strengths: Well-motivated approach using affordances to reason about occluded hand-object interactions
Systematic affordance description generation combining VLM (parsing) and LLM (summarization) steps
Substantial improvements (4.9 mm, 25% reduction) in the challenging high-occlusion regime on HOGraspNet
Demonstrates controllable generation where the diffusion model responds to affordance variations
Appropriate evaluation on a dataset with explicit occlusion and affordance annotations
weaknesses: Critical limitation inadequately addressed: the method requires ground truth grasp taxonomy at test time, but the paper provides no evidence that predicted taxonomy works and no analysis of robustness to incorrect labels. This fundamentally limits practical applicability.
Single-dataset evaluation (HOGraspNet only) with limited scale (1/10 subsampling, 300 test instances); no cross-dataset validation or generalization analysis
Weak baseline comparisons: only HaMeR regression and a simplified IHGen baseline; missing comparisons with other contextual priors, physics-informed methods, and recent hand pose work
No ablation studies on critical components: which affordance elements matter? How sensitive is the method to description quality, VLM/LLM choices, and the two-step generation scheme?
Marginal improvements outside high-occlusion cases (0.02 mm at low occlusion, 0.9 mm at medium occlusion), limiting general applicability
Insufficient analysis of method behavior: no failure case discussion, no sensitivity to description quality, occlusion detection accuracy not validated, handling of non-standard grasps unclear
Heavy reliance on recent, proprietary models (QwenVL2.5 from Feb 2025, Mistral-7B) raises reproducibility concerns; no ablation on VLM/LLM choice effects
Limited technical novelty: diffusion architecture adapted from InterHandGen [12], refinement strategy from [16]; affordance conditioning is somewhat incremental
Incomplete experimental details: diffusion training procedure, hyperparameters, computational cost not reported; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals
IHGen baseline paradoxically degrades performance at low/medium occlusion—this counterintuitive result is mentioned but not analyzed

strengths: Well-motivated and intuitive approach: The use of affordance-guided textual descriptions is well-motivated by how humans resolve ambiguities in hand-object interactions, and the extension beyond categorical labels to rich descriptions is a thoughtful design choice.

Novel application of affordances to 3D hand reconstruction: This is the first work to introduce affordance-aware textual descriptions for hand pose estimation, enriching the representation beyond existing categorical approaches with object properties and interaction intent.

Strong performance under heavy occlusion: The method achieves a 25% (4.9 mm) improvement under high occlusion compared to HaMeR, demonstrating clear practical value for the challenging scenarios where contextual reasoning is most needed.

Technically sound and well-designed pipeline: The two-stage affordance generation (VLM parsing + LLM summarization) is sensible, inspired by chain-of-thought reasoning, and the diffusion-based conditioning with CLIP embeddings is appropriately implemented.

Consistent improvements across occlusion levels: Unlike the unconditional baseline which degrades at lower occlusions, the affordance-guided approach shows monotonic improvements, suggesting the method robustly leverages contextual information.

Excellent presentation and visualization: The paper is clearly written with effective figures (especially Figures 1-3) that effectively communicate the motivation, method, and results. Qualitative results convincingly demonstrate more natural and physically plausible poses.

Demonstrated controllability: Figure 5 effectively validates that the diffusion model responds semantically to variations in affordance descriptions (e.g., adapting grasp width to object size), confirming the conditioning works as intended.

Appropriate evaluation on challenging dataset: HOGraspNet provides a realistic testbed with severe occlusions and diverse hand-object interactions, and the subsampling preserves diversity while remaining computationally tractable.
weaknesses: Critical dependency on ground truth grasp taxonomy: The paper acknowledges that VLMs struggle with grasp taxonomy classification and relies on ground truth HOGraspNet annotations. This significantly limits practical applicability, as deployment would require accurate grasp predictions from a classifier (which is itself a challenging problem). The actual affordance generation is thus incomplete in practice.

Limited evaluation scope: Evaluation is restricted to HOGraspNet. Testing on additional hand-object interaction datasets (HO3D, DexYCB, OakInk, etc.) would strengthen generalization claims. The use of 1/10 subsampling, while computationally justified, may miss important diversity.

Moderate technical novelty: The method primarily combines existing components (diffusion models, CLIP encoding, VLMs, InterHandGen architecture) for a new application. While the combination is effective, the algorithmic contributions are incremental. The refinement strategy closely follows prior work [16].

Insufficient ablation studies: No ablations isolate individual affordance components (which elements drive improvements?). Missing analysis of VLM vs. LLM contribution, and whether simpler affordance representations (e.g., direct object labels) could achieve comparable results.

Limited quantitative analysis and metrics: Only PA-MPJPE is reported. Additional metrics (raw MPJPE, mesh error, joint-wise error breakdown, kinematic feasibility) would provide a more complete picture. Absolute improvements are modest (0.23 mm average); no confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are provided. Sample size of 300 is reasonable but not large.

Occlusion detection not rigorously validated: The method's occlusion detection relies on heuristics (ray casting, SAM2 masks). No analysis of detection accuracy or its impact on final results. Errors in occlusion detection could cascade into pose errors.

Incomplete baseline comparisons: The unconditional InterHandGen baseline degrades at lower occlusions—this deserves analysis. Missing comparisons with other contextual hand pose methods (action labels, intention labels) mentioned in related work, and recent refinement approaches.

Missing computational analysis: No runtime comparison or efficiency analysis provided. Multiple VLM/LLM inferences plus iterative refinement could be expensive. Convergence behavior and computational requirements are not discussed.

Generalization concerns inadequately addressed: The method is trained on HOGraspNet's object categories and grasp types. How does it generalize to novel objects or interaction patterns? VLM affordance predictions may degrade on out-of-distribution scenarios.

Insufficient implementation details: Training data size, preprocessing, hyperparameter selection, learning rates, epochs, and convergence criteria are not specified. These omissions affect reproducibility. Diffusion step and noise schedule choices are not justified.
No code or reproducibility plan: While the work uses published models, no mention of code release or detailed reproduction instructions is provided.
